title: The Small Radiators
premise: Quentin Ishikawa, a piano tuner who believes he can hear a building's whole history through its radiators, learns that the house he grew up in — the one his family lost decades ago under circumstances no one will discuss — is going to auction. As he attends the viewing, he discovers the current owner has been receiving letters in his late father's handwriting, dated after his father's death. Quentin must untangle a forgery, an inheritance quietly stolen from his mother, and his own complicit silence, culminating in a final night in the empty house where he confronts the brother who took it all. He ends not with the house, but with the deed burned in its last working radiator, choosing to be a tenant of his own life rather than an owner of the past.
about_author: Cyrus Kavanagh is the pen name of a former building superintendent who spent twenty years listening to the pipes of old apartment blocks before turning to fiction. He writes about inheritance, architecture, and the quiet violence of families from a rented flat he refuses to buy.

chapters.title: The Pitch of Empty Rooms
chapters.summary: Third-person limited on Quentin. He tunes a piano in a wealthy client's home and reads the house's history through its radiators — marriages, arguments, a death in the back bedroom. The client asks why he never bought a place of his own; he deflects. Emotional beat: the loneliness of a man fluent in other people's homes and homeless in his own life.

chapters.title: Lot 47
chapters.summary: Quentin's sister Marisol calls: their childhood house is up for auction, and she wants him there. He resists, but attends the public viewing and hears, through the radiators, the exact afternoon everything went wrong — his father's voice, his brother Daniel's, a slammed door. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into compulsion.

chapters.title: Letters from a Dead Man
chapters.summary: The current owner, an elderly widow named Mrs. Okonkwo, mentions strange letters she's received, signed by Quentin's father — postmarked years after his death. Quentin recognizes the handwriting instantly: it's Daniel's. POV: Quentin, with a flashback to childhood forgery games. Emotional beat: the past is not just alive; it's impersonating the dead.

chapters.title: What Mother Signed
chapters.summary: Quentin visits his mother, Ada, in a care facility. Fragments emerge: she transferred the deed decades ago to protect someone, believing she'd get it back. She calls Daniel 'the good one' with unsettling serenity. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: grief curdling into anger as he realizes his mother was deceived and he looked away.

chapters.title: The Tenant's Almanac
chapters.summary: A quieter interlude. Quentin tunes pianos across the city, cataloguing houses that hum with honesty and houses that lie through their pipes. He drafts, then burns, a letter to Daniel. Marisol presses him to bid at auction; he refuses. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: the false calm before the descent — avoidance dressed as peace.

chapters.title: Rerouted
chapters.summary: The city announces the last bus route through the old neighborhood will be permanently rerouted. Quentin rides it one final time, past shuttered storefronts, and realizes the geography of his childhood is being erased faster than the truth about it. He decides to confront Daniel before the auction. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: urgency — a deadline imposed by the world, not the family.

chapters.title: The Good One
chapters.summary: Quentin finds Daniel in a suburban kitchen that mimics their childhood home down to the radiator covers. Daniel admits the forged letters — sent to Mrs. Okonkwo to keep the house's history 'warm' for a buyer — and claims he took the deed to save Ada from creditors. POV: Quentin, then a destabilizing shift into Daniel's account. Emotional beat: the seductive logic of a corrupt man, and Quentin's horrifying flicker of belief.

chapters.title: Auction
chapters.summary: The auction. Daniel bids; Marisol bids; Quentin, having emptied his savings, bids against both. Mrs. Okonkwo appears and publicly reads one of the forged letters aloud, and the room turns. Daniel withdraws in fury. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: public exposure as climax — the family's secret performed in front of strangers.

chapters.title: The Last Night of the House
chapters.summary: Before the transfer, Quentin spends one night alone in the house, listening to every radiator. In the cold basement he finds his father's real last letter — to him, not Daniel — asking him to protect his mother and admitting his own failures. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: reckoning; the house finally speaks plainly, and so must he.

chapters.title: Tenant
chapters.summary: Quentin signs the deed over to Mrs. Okonkwo, who lost her own home to a forged will years ago, and burns the forged letters in the house's last working radiator. He takes a room as a renter near Marisol and begins teaching piano tuning to kids from the old neighborhood. POV: Quentin. Emotional beat: release — power renounced, identity chosen, inheritance transformed into something given rather than held.
